questions.prompt: In React, why does a list of items need a stable key prop?

options.text: So React can match elements to state across re-renders
To sort the list automatically
To make the list accessible to screen readers
To cache the list in localStorage

questions.explanation: Keys let React identify which item is which between renders. Using the array index as a key breaks when items are inserted or reordered, because state stays attached to the position rather than the item.

questions.prompt: What does the CSS box-sizing: border-box setting change?

options.text: It centres the element horizontally
Padding and border are included in the declared width
It removes the element's margin
It makes the element position: absolute

questions.explanation: With the default content-box, padding and border are added on top of the width. border-box includes them, which is why a 50% wide box with padding stops overflowing its container.

questions.prompt: Why does a click handler's console.log run before a fetch .then() that was called first?

options.text: fetch always takes at least one second
Click handlers have higher CPU priority
Promise callbacks are queued and run after the current synchronous work
console.log is synchronous but fetch is not supported

questions.explanation: JavaScript runs the current call stack to completion first. Promise resolutions are queued as microtasks and only run once the stack is empty, so synchronous code always wins.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the dependency array in React's useEffect?

options.text: It lists which npm packages the effect needs
It sets how many times the effect may run
It orders effects within a component
It controls when the effect re-runs by comparing values between renders

questions.explanation: React compares each dependency to its previous value and re-runs the effect only when one changed. An empty array runs it once; omitting the array runs it after every render.

questions.prompt: Which best describes the difference between localStorage and sessionStorage?

options.text: sessionStorage is cleared when the tab closes; localStorage persists
localStorage is encrypted; sessionStorage is not
sessionStorage is shared across all domains
localStorage is sent with every HTTP request

questions.explanation: Both are origin-scoped and unencrypted. The difference is lifetime: sessionStorage dies with the tab, localStorage survives until it is cleared. Neither is sent with requests, unlike cookies.

questions.prompt: In flexbox, what does justify-content control?

options.text: Alignment along the cross axis
Whether items wrap onto a new line
Alignment along the main axis
The order in which items are painted

questions.explanation: justify-content distributes items along the main axis, which flex-direction determines. align-items handles the cross axis, which is the pair most often confused.

questions.prompt: What problem does React's virtual DOM actually solve?

options.text: It makes JavaScript execution faster than native code
It batches and minimises expensive real DOM mutations
It removes the need for CSS
It renders pages on the server only

questions.explanation: Touching the real DOM triggers layout and paint. React diffs a cheap in-memory tree and applies the minimum set of real mutations. It is not faster than hand-tuned direct DOM work, just far easier to get right.

questions.prompt: Why is using a div with an onClick handler worse than a real button for accessibility?

options.text: A div cannot be styled to look like a button
Click events do not fire on a div
Divs are slower to render
It is not focusable and not announced as a control

questions.explanation: A button is keyboard focusable, activates on Enter and Space, and is announced as a button by assistive technology. A div gets none of that unless you rebuild it all by hand.

questions.prompt: What is a debounce typically used for on the frontend?

options.text: Delaying work until input has stopped for a set period
Retrying a failed request automatically
Compressing images before upload
Preventing cross-site scripting

questions.explanation: Debouncing waits for a quiet period before acting, which is why a search box fires one request after typing stops instead of one per keystroke. Throttling instead caps the rate.

questions.prompt: Why does CORS block a request that Postman completes fine?

options.text: Postman uses a faster network stack
CORS is a browser-enforced policy, and Postman is not a browser
The server rejects requests without a UI
Postman automatically disables HTTPS

questions.explanation: CORS is enforced by the browser to protect a user's credentials on other origins. The server still received the request; the browser refused to hand the response to your JavaScript.

questions.prompt: What does semantic HTML mean in practice?

options.text: Writing all markup in lowercase
Avoiding inline styles
Choosing elements that describe their content, such as nav and article
Minifying HTML before deploying

questions.explanation: Semantic elements carry meaning that browsers, assistive technology and search engines can use. A page built entirely from divs looks identical but conveys no structure.

questions.prompt: In JavaScript, what is a closure?

options.text: A function that keeps access to variables from where it was defined
A way to close a browser tab from script
A method that ends a network connection
A loop that always terminates

questions.explanation: A closure captures its defining scope, so the inner function can still read those variables after the outer function returned. This is what makes counters and private state work.

questions.prompt: What does code splitting achieve in a frontend bundle?

options.text: It removes all unused CSS
It defers loading code until the route that needs it
It converts JavaScript to WebAssembly
It duplicates code for redundancy

questions.explanation: Splitting the bundle means the initial page ships only what it needs, and other chunks load on demand. It is the main lever on time-to-interactive for a large app.

questions.prompt: Why can two elements with the same specificity behave differently in CSS?

options.text: Rules are applied alphabetically by selector
The browser picks one at random
Later rules in source order win
The shorter selector always wins

questions.explanation: When specificity ties, the cascade falls back to source order and the last declaration wins. This is why stylesheet import order changes behaviour without any selector changing.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of rendering user-supplied HTML with dangerouslySetInnerHTML?

options.text: It slows down rendering significantly
It breaks server-side rendering
It disables React's key checking
It allows cross-site scripting if the input is not sanitised

questions.explanation: React escapes text by default, which is what prevents XSS. Bypassing that with raw HTML means any injected script tag or event handler executes with the user's session.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript?

options.text: === compares values without type coercion
== only works on numbers
=== compares memory addresses only
There is no difference in modern JavaScript

questions.explanation: == coerces operands before comparing, so '1' == 1 is true and surprises follow. === requires matching types, which is why it is the default recommendation.

questions.prompt: In React, what is lifting state up?

options.text: Storing state in localStorage
Moving shared state to the closest common ancestor
Using a global variable outside React
Moving state into a useRef to avoid re-renders

questions.explanation: When two siblings need the same value, it moves to their common parent and flows down as props. Duplicating it in both is what causes the two to drift out of sync.

questions.prompt: What does a Content Security Policy header do?

options.text: Encrypts the response body
Compresses assets before sending
Restricts which sources the page may load scripts and styles from
Forces the browser to use HTTP/2

questions.explanation: CSP declares the allowed origins for scripts, styles and other resources, so an injected script from an unapproved host is blocked. It is a second line of defence behind proper escaping.

questions.prompt: Why might a component re-render even though its props look unchanged?

options.text: React re-renders every component on a timer
The parent re-rendered, and a new object or function prop was created
The browser window lost focus
CSS changed on the element

questions.explanation: An inline object or arrow function is a new reference on every parent render, so a shallow comparison sees it as changed. useMemo and useCallback exist to keep those references stable.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of server-side rendering for a content site?

options.text: It removes the need for JavaScript entirely
It makes the server cheaper to run
It guarantees the page never changes
Faster first paint and content crawlers can read

questions.explanation: The browser receives real markup instead of an empty shell, so content appears sooner and does not depend on JavaScript running for indexing. The cost is server work per request.

questions.prompt: What does the defer attribute on a script tag do?

options.text: Downloads the script in parallel and runs it after parsing completes
Stops the script from ever loading
Runs the script before the HTML is parsed
Loads the script only on user interaction

questions.explanation: defer lets the parser continue while the script downloads, then executes it in document order before DOMContentLoaded. async also downloads in parallel but runs as soon as it arrives, in any order.

questions.prompt: Which approach correctly makes a layout responsive without JavaScript?

options.text: Detecting the user agent string and swapping stylesheets
Using media queries and relative units
Setting a fixed pixel width for every breakpoint
Rendering a separate mobile site

questions.explanation: Media queries respond to the actual viewport, and relative units let content adapt between breakpoints. User-agent sniffing is brittle and misses resized desktop windows entirely.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a source map in a production build?

options.text: It compresses the bundle further
It lists every network request the page makes
It maps minified code back to the original source for debugging
It stores the application's routing table

questions.explanation: A source map lets the browser show a readable stack trace against original files despite the shipped code being minified. Whether to expose it publicly is a separate decision.

questions.prompt: Why is storing a JWT in localStorage considered riskier than in an httpOnly cookie?

options.text: localStorage has a much smaller size limit
Cookies are encrypted by default
localStorage is cleared on refresh
Any injected script can read localStorage, but not an httpOnly cookie

questions.explanation: An httpOnly cookie is invisible to JavaScript, so an XSS payload cannot exfiltrate it. localStorage is fully readable by any script on the page. Cookies then need CSRF protection in exchange.

questions.prompt: What does the browser's repaint versus reflow distinction mean for performance?

options.text: Reflow recalculates layout and is more expensive than repaint
Repaint recalculates geometry; reflow only changes colour
Both are equally cheap in modern browsers
Reflow only happens on page load

questions.explanation: Changing a colour repaints; changing size or position forces the browser to recompute layout for affected elements. Animating transform and opacity avoids reflow, which is why they stay smooth.
